nodes.name: Rapid decay of non-constant terms of Eisenstein series
nodes.statement: For any $\Phi \in \mathcal{S}(\ag{A}^2)$, $m \in \ag{N}$ and any $\sigma > \norm[\Re s]$, we have $$ \extnorm{\frac{\partial^m}{\partial s^m} \left( {\rm E}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\Phi)(g) - {\rm E}_{\gp{N}}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\Phi)(g) \right)} \leq \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbf{F}^{\times}} \extnorm{\frac{\partial^m}{\partial s^m} W_{\Phi}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};a(\alpha)g)} \ll_{\sigma,\Phi} {\rm Ht}(g)^{-\frac{1}{2}-\sigma}, $$ which is of rapid decay with respect to ${\rm Ht}(g)$.
conclusions: which is of rapid decay with respect to ${\rm Ht}(g)$.
nodes.statement_short: $s$-derivatives of $E-E_N$ are bounded by the sum of Whittaker functions, $\ll\mathrm{Ht}(g)^{-1/2-\sigma}$: rapid decay in the height.
nodes.label: GlobRDEisWhi

nodes.name: K-isotypic Fourier expansion of f
nodes.statement:
Consider $f \in V_{\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}}^{\infty}$ and take its Fourier expansion into $\gp{K}$-isotypic types
	$$ f = \sum_{\vec{n}} \hat{f}_{\vec{n}} \cdot e_{\vec{n}}(\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}) $$
for some $\hat{f}_{\vec{n}} \in \ag{C}$, where $e_{\vec{n}}(\xi,\omega\xi^{-1})$ is unitary with $\gp{K}$-type parametrized by $\vec{n}$ as in \cite[Section 3.5]{Wu5}.

nodes.name: Intertwining coefficients mu(s; n)
Poles of intertwining coefficients
nodes.statement: The possible poles of the collection of meromorphic functions $\{ \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n}) : \vec{n} \}$ are \begin{itemize} \item The pole of $\Lambda(1-2s,\omega\xi^{-2})$ at $s=(1+i\mu(\omega\xi^{-2}))/2$ with order at most $1$, when $\omega\xi^{-2}$ is trivial on $\ag{A}^{(1)}$ and $\vec{n}=\vec{0}$. We call this pole the \emph{spherical pole}. \item The (both trivial and non-trivial) zeros of $L(1+2s,\omega^{-1}\xi^2)$ with order at most that of the zero. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: The coefficients $\mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec n)$ have at most the spherical pole and poles at zeros of $L(1+2s,\omega^{-1}\xi^2)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.31
nodes.statement: This can be seen either from our explicit computation of $\mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n})$ in \cite{Wu5}, or from (\ref{RelSec}) and $$ \mathcal{M} f_{\Phi}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}) = f_{\widehat{\Phi}}(-s,\omega\xi^{-1},\xi), $$ which is meromorphic with a simple pole at $s=(1+i\mu(\omega\xi^{-2}))/2$ (the other pole is cancelled by that of $f_{\Phi}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1})$) by Tate's theory.
nodes.statement_short: From the explicit computation in [Wu5], or from (5.1) and Tate's theory for $\mathcal M f_\Phi$.

nodes.name: Polynomial bound for intertwining coefficients
nodes.statement: Assume $\mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n}_0)$ has a pole at $s_0$ with order $n$ ($n=0$ if it is holomorphic at $s_0$) for some $\vec{n}_0$. Define $$ \Norm[\vec{n}] = \prod_v (\norm[n_v]+1) \text{ for } \vec{n} = (n_v)_v. $$ Then as $s$ lying in any small compact neighborhood $K$ of $s_0$ where no other pole occur, we have $$ \extnorm{(s-s_0)^n \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n})} \ll \Norm[\vec{n}]^N $$ for some $N$ and the implied constant depending only on $K$, $\xi$ and $\omega\xi^{-1}$ (i.e., independent of $\vec{n}$).
assumptions: Assume $\mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n}_0)$ has a pole at $s_0$ with order $n$ ($n=0$ if it is holomorphic at $s_0$) for some $\vec{n}_0$.
conclusions: $$ \extnorm{(s-s_0)^n \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n})} \ll \Norm[\vec{n}]^N $$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.32
nodes.statement_short: Explicit formulas from [Wu5] plus an elementary product bound.

nodes.name: Expansion of the constant term near a pole
nodes.statement:
Under the condition of the lemma we have $$ (s-s_0)^n {m E}_{\gp{N}}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f) = (s-s_0)^n f(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}) + \sum_{\vec{n}} \hat{f}_{\vec{n}} \cdot (s-s_0)^n \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n}) e_{\vec{n}}(-s,\omega\xi^{-1},\xi). $$ Consequently, for any $m \in \ag{N}$, $y \in \ag{A}^{	imes}$ and $\kappa \in \gp{K}$ we can write  egin{align*} &\quad  rac{d^m}{d s^m} \mid_{s=s_0} (s-s_0)^n {m E}_{\gp{N}}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)(a(y)\kappa) \ &=  rac{m!}{(m-n)!} 
orm[y]_{\ag{A}}^{ rac{1}{2}+s_0} \xi(y) (\log 
orm[y]_{\ag{A}})^{m-n} f(\kappa) + \sum_{k=0}^m 
orm[y]_{\ag{A}}^{ rac{1}{2}-s_0} \omega\xi^{-1}(y) (\log 
orm[y]_{\ag{A}})^k f_k(\kappa), \end{align*} where $(\log 
orm[y]_{\ag{A}})^{m-n}$ is understood as $0$ if $m<n$ and where the maps $$ V_{\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}}^{\infty} 	o V_{\omega\xi^{-1},\xi}^{\infty}, f 	o f_k 	ext{ for } 0 \leq k \leq m $$ are $\gp{K}$-maps and continuous with respect to the Sobolev norms on $\gp{K}_{\infty}$.
assumptions: Under the condition of the lemma we have
nodes.statement_short: Near a pole $s_0$, $(s-s_0)^nE_N$ has a convergent $K$-type expansion, and its $s$-derivatives are explicit combinations of $|y|^{1/2\pm s_0}\log^k|y|$ with continuous $K$-maps.
nodes.label: GlobRDEisCst

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.33
nodes.statement: The lemma shows that $(s-s_0)^n \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n})$ is polynomially increasing in $\vec{n}$. But $\hat{f}_{\vec{n}}$ is rapidly decreasing in $\vec{n}$ by smoothness of $f$. The sum over $\vec{n}$ is thus absolutely and uniformly convergent for $s$ lying in $K$, hence defines an analytic function in $s$. By uniqueness of analytic continuation, we get the first equation. The rest follows from the polynomial increase of $(s-s_0)^n \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n})$ and Cauchy's integral formula for derivatives.
nodes.statement_short: Polynomial growth of coefficients (Lemma 5.32) against rapid decay of $\hat f_{\vec n}$ gives uniform convergence; analytic continuation and Cauchy's formula finish.

nodes.name: Constant term at the spherical pole
nodes.statement: If $s_0$ is the spherical pole, then $n=1$ and for $m=0$ we have $f_k=0$ unless $k=0$. Then $$ f_0(\kappa) = \lim_{s \to s_0} \frac{(s-s_0)\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(2(s_0-s)}{\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(2-2(s_0-s)))} \int_{\gp{K}} f(\kappa) d\kappa = - \frac{\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^*(0)}{\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(2)} \int_{\gp{K}} f(\kappa) d\kappa. $$

nodes.name: Integers r, N
nodes.statement: Let $r,N \in \ag{N}, r,N \geq 2$.

nodes.name: Principal congruence subgroup
nodes.statement:
It is well-known that there is an exact sequence
	$$ 1 \to \Gamma(N) \to {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z}) \to {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z}/N\ag{Z}) \to 1, $$
	where $\Gamma(N)$ is called the principal congruence subgroup of ${\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$ modulo $N$.

nodes.name: Congruence subgroups Gamma_0(N)
nodes.statement: The pre-image of the upper resp. lower triangular subgroup of ${\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z}/N\ag{Z})$ in ${\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$ is denoted by $\Gamma_0(N)$ resp. $\Gamma_0^-(N)$, which includes $\Gamma(N)$ as a normal subgroup.

nodes.name: Unipotent matrices n_r^+-
Unipotent coset representatives for Gamma_0(N)
nodes.statement: Any coset of $\Gamma_0(N) \backslash {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$ resp. $\Gamma_0^-(N) \backslash {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$ has a representative of the form $N_- N_+$ resp. $N_+N_-$, where $N_-$ resp. $N_+$ is lower resp. upper unipotent with off-diagonal entries lying in $[-\frac{N}{2}, \frac{N}{2}] \cap \ag{Z}$.
conclusions: has a representative of the form $N_- N_+$ resp. $N_+N_-$, where $N_-$ resp. $N_+$ is lower resp. upper unipotent with off-diagonal entries lying in $[-\frac{N}{2}, \frac{N}{2}] \cap \ag{Z}$
nodes.label: CongGpLemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.35
nodes.statement: We treat the case for $\Gamma_0(N)$. Take any $A \in {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$. Let the first column of $A$ be $(a_1,\cdots,a_r)^T \in \ag{Z}^r$. Then we have ${\rm lcd}(a_1,\cdots,a_r)=1$, which implies the existence of $u_i \in \ag{Z}$ such that $\Sigma_{i=1}^r u_i a_i = 1$. In particular, we have ${\rm lcd}(u_1,a_2,\cdots,a_r)=1$. For any $k_j \in \ag{Z}, 2 \leq j \leq r$, the substitution $$ u_1' = u_1+\sum_{j=2}^r k_j a_j; u_j' = u_j-k_j, 2 \leq j \leq r $$ still gives $\Sigma_{i=1}^r u_i' a_i = 1$. By an iterative application of Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progression, we can choose $k_j$'s such that $u_1'$ is a prime number as large as we want. In particular, we can make ${\rm lcd}(u_1',N)=1$. Since ${\rm lcd}(u_1',\cdots,u_r')=1$, at least one of $u_j', 2 \leq j \leq r$, say $u_2'$, is coprime with $u_1'$. Hence ${\rm lcd}(u_1',Nu_2')=1$ and we can find $v_1,v_2 \in \ag{Z}$ such that $u_1'v_2-Nu_2'v_1=1$. The matrix $$ B = \begin{pmatrix} u_1' & u_2' & u_3' \cdots \\ Nv_1 & v_2 & 0 \cdots \\ \vec{0} & \vec{0} & I_{r-2} \end{pmatrix} \in \Gamma_0(N) $$ and gives, for some $A'=\tilde{A}-\vec{\alpha} \vec{\beta_1}^T \in {\rm SL}_{r-1}(\ag{Z})$, that $$ BA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \vec{\beta_1}^T \\ \vec{\alpha} & \tilde{A} \end{pmatrix} \Rightarrow A \in \Gamma_0(N) \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \\ \vec{\alpha} & A' \end{pmatrix} n_r^+(\vec{\beta_1}). $$ Repeating the process on $A'$ or making an induction on $r$ we then find successively $\vec{\beta_k} \in \ag{Z}^{r-k}$ such that for some lower unipotent $N_-^1$ $$ A \in \Gamma_0(N) N_-^1 N_+^1, N_+^1=\prod_{k=0}^{r-2} \begin{pmatrix} I_k & 0 \\ 0 & n_{r-k}^+(\vec{\beta_{k+1}}) \end{pmatrix}. $$ Taking $N_-$ resp. $N_+$ with off-diagonal entries lying in $[-\frac{N}{2}, \frac{N}{2}] \cap \ag{Z}$ such that $N_-^1 \equiv N_- \pmod{N}$ resp. $N_+^1 \equiv N_+ \pmod{N}$, we then find $N_-^1 N_-^{-1}, N_+^1 N_+^{-1} \in \Gamma(N)$ and conclude by its normality.
nodes.statement_short: Use Dirichlet's theorem to make a Bezout coefficient prime to $N$, build an explicit $B\in\Gamma_0(N)$ clearing the first column, induct on $r$ and reduce mod $N$. Key step: the prime choice of $u_1'$.

nodes.name: Degree r = r_1 + 2 r_2
nodes.statement: Let $[\mathbf{F}:\ag{Q}]=r=r_1+2r_2$ where $r_1$ resp. $2r_2$ is the number of embeddings of $\mathbf{F}$ into real resp. complex numbers.

nodes.name: Canonical embedding sigma
nodes.statement:
Recall that we have a canonical map by choosing one complex embedding $\sigma_{r_1+j}, 1 \leq j \leq r_2$ in a pair conjugate to each other by complex conjugation
	$$ \sigma: \mathbf{F} \to \ag{R}^{r_1} \times \ag{C}^{r_2} \simeq \ag{R}^r, $$
	$$ \sigma(x) = (\sigma_1(x), \cdots, \sigma_{r_1+r_2}(x)) = (\sigma_1(x), \cdots, \sigma_{r_1}(x), \Re \sigma_{r_1+1}(x), \Im \sigma_{r_1+1}(x), \cdots, \Re \sigma_{r_1+r_2}(x), \Im \sigma_{r_1+r_2}(x)). $$

nodes.name: sigma(J) is a lattice
nodes.statement: For every fractional ideal $\mathfrak{J}$, $\sigma(\mathfrak{J})$ is then a $\ag{Z}$-lattice of $\ag{R}^r$.

nodes.name: Test function f_c
nodes.statement:
For $c \gg 1$, we define a functions $f_c$ on $\ag{R}^{r_1} \times \ag{C}^{r_2}$ by
	$$ f_c(\vec{x}) = \prod_{i=1}^{r_1} \min(1, \norm[x_i]^{-c}) \prod_{j=1}^{r_2} \min(1, \norm[x_{r_1+j}]^{-2c}), \vec{x}=(x_i)_{1\leq i \leq r_1+r_2}. $$

nodes.name: Lattice sum estimates

conclusions: $ \sum_{\alpha \in \mathfrak{J}^{-1} - \{0\}} f_c(t\sigma(\alpha)) \ll_{\mathbf{F},c} \norm[\mathfrak{o}/\mathfrak{J}]^{3c} t^{-c} $
$ \sum_{\alpha \in \mathfrak{J}^{-1}} f_c(t\sigma(\alpha)) \ll_{\mathbf{F},c} t^{-r} \norm[\mathfrak{o}/\mathfrak{J}]^{-1} \left( 1+t\frac{\norm[\mathfrak{o}/\mathfrak{J}]^2}{\sqrt{r}} \right)^{rc} $
$ \sum_{\alpha \in \mathfrak{J}^{-1} - \{0\}} f_c(t\sigma(\alpha)) \ll_{\mathbf{F},c} \norm[\mathfrak{o}/\mathfrak{J}]^{3c} t^{-c} $
$ \sum_{\alpha \in \mathfrak{J}^{-1}} f_c(t\sigma(\alpha)) \ll_{\mathbf{F},c} t^{-r} \norm[\mathfrak{o}/\mathfrak{J}]^{-1} \left( 1+t\frac{\norm[\mathfrak{o}/\mathfrak{J}]^2}{\sqrt{r}} \right)^{rc} $
nodes.statement_short: Bounds for sums of $f_c(t\sigma(\alpha))$ over a fractional ideal lattice, polynomial in $|\mathfrak o/\mathfrak J|$.
nodes.label: GTechEstClassical

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.36
nodes.statement_short: (1) compare $f_c$ with lattice norms, bounding the basis change via elementary divisors and Lemma 5.35; (2) compare the sum with the integral over fundamental parallelograms.

nodes.name: Valuation v(J) of an ideal
nodes.statement:
We shall write, denoting by $\mathfrak{p}_v$ the prime ideal corresponding to $v<\infty$, $v(\mathfrak{J}) \in \ag{N}$ such that
	$$ \mathfrak{J} = \prod_{v<\infty} \mathfrak{p}_v^{v(\mathfrak{J})}. $$

nodes.name: Adelic lattice sum estimate
nodes.statement_short: Adelic version of Lemma 5.36: the sum over $\alpha\in\mathbf F^\times$ of local min-type weights is bounded polynomially in $|y|_{\mathbb A}$ and $|\mathfrak o/\mathfrak J|$.
nodes.label: GTechEst

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.37
nodes.statement_short: Normalize $y$ by class group representatives and units (Dirichlet's unit theorem) to reduce to the classical lattice sum, then apply Lemma 5.36.

nodes.name: Assume the contrary
nodes.statement_short: Assume some $\Re\alpha_i\ge1/2$ and write out $\int_1^T f\,dt/t^2$, which must stay bounded.

nodes.name: Maximal real part
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma = \max_j \Re \alpha_j$. We distinguish two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Let $\sigma=\max\Re\alpha_j$ and split into two cases.

nodes.name: Case sigma = 1/2
nodes.statement_short: Normalize by $(\log T)^l$ to get $\lim\sum c_jT^{i\tau_j}=0$ with distinct $\tau_j$.

nodes.name: Case sigma > 1/2
nodes.statement: (2) $\sigma > 1/2$. Let $l=\max \{ n_j: \Re \alpha_j = \sigma \}$. We divide both sides of the equation by $T^{\sigma-1/2} (\log T)^l$ and let $T \to +\infty$ to get an equation of the same form as (\ref{AbsEq}).
nodes.statement_short: Normalize by $T^{\sigma-1/2}(\log T)^l$ to get the same kind of equation.

nodes.name: Contradiction with Corollary 2.4
nodes.statement: We conclude because (\ref{AbsEq}) contradicts the following Corollary \ref{ErgodicLemma}.
nodes.statement_short: The limit equation contradicts Corollary 2.4.

nodes.name: Characters of the torus
nodes.statement:
Consider the group of characters ${\rm Ch}(\ag{T}^n)$ of $\ag{T}^n$ given by
	$$ e_{\vec{n}}(\vec{x}) = e(\vec{n} \cdot \vec{x}) = e(\sum_{i=1}^n n_i x_i), \vec{n} \in \ag{N}^n, \vec{x} \in \ag{R}^n $$
where $e(x) = e^{2\pi i x}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the characters $e_{\vec n}$ of $\mathbb T^n$.

nodes.name: Pontryagin duality
nodes.statement: By the duality theorem for locally compact abelian groups, the group of characters ${\rm Ch}(\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}})$ is the quotient of ${\rm Ch}(\ag{T}^n)$ by the subgroup of $e_{\vec{n}}$'s which vanish on $\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Characters of $\mathbb T_{\vec\theta}$ are a quotient of those of $\mathbb T^n$.

nodes.name: Identify trivial characters
nodes.statement:
Obviously, we have
	$$ e_{\vec{n}}(\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}})=1 \Leftrightarrow e(t\vec{n} \cdot \vec{\theta}) = 1 \text{ for } \forall t \in \ag{R} \Leftrightarrow \vec{n} \cdot \vec{\theta}=0. $$
	So ${\rm Ch}(\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}})$ are $e_{\vec{n}}$'s modulo the subgroup of $e_{\vec{n}}$'s with $\vec{n} \cdot \vec{\theta}=0$.
nodes.statement_short: $e_{\vec n}$ is trivial on $\mathbb T_{\vec\theta}$ iff $\vec n\cdot\vec\theta=0$.

nodes.name: Averages of nontrivial characters
nodes.statement:
Let $[e_{\vec{n}}] 
eq 0$ denote a non trivial equivalence class of $e_{\vec{n}}$ in the quotient group, we calculate
	$$ \extnorm{  rac{1}{T} \int_0^T [e_{\vec{n}}]( [\vec{x}] + [t\vec{	heta}] ) dt } = \extnorm{  rac{e(\vec{n} \cdot \vec{x})}{T} \cdot  rac{e(T\vec{n} \cdot \vec{	heta} ) - 1}{\vec{n} \cdot \vec{	heta}} } \leq  rac{2}{
orm[T] \cdot 
orm[\vec{n} \cdot \vec{	heta}]} 	o 0, T 	o \infty. $$
nodes.statement_short: Time averages of a non-trivial character tend to $0$.

nodes.name: Stone-Weierstrass
nodes.statement: The lemma is thus proved for $f = [e_{\vec{n}}]$, hence the $\ag{C}$-vector space generated by ${\rm Ch}(\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}})$, which is also a $*$-subalgebra of ${\rm C}(\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}})$. The lemma then follows by a standard application of the complex version of the Stone-Weierstrass theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Extend from characters to all continuous functions by Stone-Weierstrass.

nodes.name: Rewrite on the torus
nodes.statement: Note that $f(e^{2\pi t}) = \sum_{k=1}^n a_k e(t\theta_k), t \in \ag{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $f(e^{2\pi t})$ as a function of $[t\vec\theta]$.

nodes.name: Assume f non-constant
nodes.statement: If $f$ is not constant, we can find $t_1, t_2 \in \ag{R}$ s.t. $f(e^{2\pi t_1}) \neq f(e^{2\pi t_2})$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $t_1,t_2$ with different values.

nodes.name: Separating neighbourhoods
nodes.statement:
By continuity, we then find some neighborhood $U_1$ of $[t_1 \vec{\theta}]$, and $U_2$ of $[t_2 \vec{\theta}]$ such that
	$$ \sum_{k=1}^n a_k e(x_k) \neq \sum_{k=1}^n a_k e(y_k), \forall \vec{x} \in U_1, \vec{y} \in U_2. $$
nodes.statement_short: Choose neighbourhoods $U_1,U_2$ on which the values differ.

nodes.name: Flow visits both
nodes.statement: But the flow $\gamma(t) = [t\vec{\theta}]$ meets both $U_1$ and $U_2$ infinitely often by the lemma, hence $\lim_{t \to \infty} f(e^{2\pi t})$ can not exist, contradicting the hypothesis.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 2.3 the flow meets both infinitely often, so no limit exists.

nodes.name: Case c <= 0 and Siegel domain bound
nodes.statement: If $c \leq 0$, then it is easy to see that $\varphi$ is bounded, since elements of bounded height in a Siegel domain form a compact subset and $\varphi$ is continuous. The same argument shows that if $c<0$ we can assume $\norm[\varphi(g)] \ll {\rm Ht}(g)^c$ to hold in a whole Siegel domain $S$ containing a fundamental domain.
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi$ is bounded for $c\le0$, and for $c<0$ the bound holds on a whole Siegel domain.

nodes.name: Translate into the Siegel domain
nodes.statement:
If ${\rm Ht}(g)$ is small, we take $\gamma \in {\rm GL}_2(\mathbf{F})$ such that $\gamma g \in S$, thus by the lemma we get
	$$ \norm[\varphi(g)] = \norm[\varphi(\gamma g)] \ll {\rm Ht}(\gamma g)^c \leq {\rm Ht}(g)^{-c}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Move $g$ into $S$ by $\gamma$ and apply Lemma 2.9.

nodes.name: Scope of the proof
nodes.statement: Since the proofs of (1) to (3) are quite similar to that in \cite{Za82}, we only mention some essential points of them. Only (4) needs more explanation.
nodes.statement_short: (1)-(3) follow Zagier; only (4) is detailed.

nodes.name: Part (1): unfolding
nodes.statement:
(1) This is standard Rankin-Selberg unfolding together with
	$$ \Lambda^T {\rm E}(s,f_0)(g) = \sum_{\gamma \in \gp{B}(\mathbf{F}) \backslash {\rm GL}_2(\mathbf{F})} f_{0,s}(\gamma g) 1_{{\rm Ht}(\gamma g) \leq T} - \sum_{\gamma \in \gp{B}(\mathbf{F}) \backslash {\rm GL}_2(\mathbf{F})} \mathcal{M} f_{0,s}(\gamma g) 1_{{\rm Ht}(\gamma g) > T}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Rankin-Selberg unfolding with the truncated Eisenstein series.

nodes.name: Part (2): rewriting
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite both terms of (1) using $R(s,\varphi)$ and $h_T$.

nodes.name: Part (3): limit T to infinity
nodes.statement: (3) In the case $\Re \alpha_i < 0$ for all $i$, we let $T \to \infty$, taking into account Proposition \ref{GlobRDEisWhi} and $h_T(s) \to 0$, to get the asserted equation.
nodes.statement_short: Let $T\to\infty$ using Proposition 5.30.

nodes.name: Part (4): residue at 1/2
nodes.statement:
(4) The integrability of $\varphi$ implies $\Re \alpha_i < 1/2$ for all $i$ by Lemma \ref{IntExpBd}. We take residue at $s=1/2$ on both sides of the equation obtained in (2) and divide by $\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(1+2s)$ to see for $T \gg 1$
\begin{align*}
	&\quad {\rm Res}_{s=\frac{1}{2}} R(s,\varphi) + {\rm Res}_{s=\frac{1}{2}} h_T(s) + \lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^{(-1)}(0) h_T(-\frac{1}{2}) \\
	&= \lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^{(-1)}(0) \int_{\mathcal{D}_T} \varphi(g)dg + {\rm Res}_{s=\frac{1}{2}} \int_{\mathcal{D}-\mathcal{D}_T} \varphi(g) \left( {\rm E}(s,f_0)(g) - {\rm E}(s,f_0)_N(g) \right) dg \\
	&\quad + \lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^{(-1)}(0) \int_T^{\infty} (a(t,\varphi)-f(t)) \frac{dt}{t^2},
\end{align*}
	where $\mathcal{D}$ is the standard fundamental domain for $[{\rm PGL}_2]$ and $\mathcal{D}_T$ is the set of $g \in \mathcal{D}$ such that ${\rm Ht}(g) \leq T$. It is easy to see that as $T \to \infty$
	$$ h_T(-\frac{1}{2}) \to 0; \quad \int_T^{\infty} (a(t,\varphi)-f(t)) \frac{dt}{t^2} \to 0. $$
	By Proposition \ref{GlobRDEisWhi}, ${\rm E}(s,f_0)(g) - {\rm E}(s,f_0)_N(g)$ is of uniformly rapid decay with respect to ${\rm Ht}(g), g \in \mathcal{D}$ as $s$ remains in a compact neighborhood of $1/2$. Hence
	$$ \int_{\mathcal{D}-\mathcal{D}_T} \varphi(g) \left( {\rm E}(s,f_0)(g) - {\rm E}(s,f_0)_N(g) \right) dg $$
	is holomorphic at $s=1/2$. We compute ${\rm Res}_{s=\frac{1}{2}} h_T(s)$ by noting that the second summand of
	$$ \frac{d^n}{d s^n} \left( \frac{T^s}{s} \right) = \frac{(-1)^n n!}{s^{n+1}} + \int_0^{\log T} t^n e^{st} dt $$
is holomorphic at $s=0$, and get
	$$ {\rm Res}_{s=\frac{1}{2}} h_T(s) = c_i \delta_{\substack{\alpha_i=-\frac{1}{2} \\ n_i=0}}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Take residues at $s=1/2$ in (2) and let $T\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Exponent bound
nodes.statement: (4) The integrability of $\varphi$ implies $\Re \alpha_i < 1/2$ for all $i$ by Lemma \ref{IntExpBd}.
nodes.statement_short: Integrability gives $\Re\alpha_i<1/2$ by Lemma 2.2.

nodes.name: Take residues
nodes.statement:
We take residue at $s=1/2$ on both sides of the equation obtained in (2) and divide by $\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(1+2s)$ to see for $T \gg 1$
\begin{align*}
	&\quad {\rm Res}_{s=\frac{1}{2}} R(s,\varphi) + {\rm Res}_{s=\frac{1}{2}} h_T(s) + \lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^{(-1)}(0) h_T(-\frac{1}{2}) \\
	&= \lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^{(-1)}(0) \int_{\mathcal{D}_T} \varphi(g)dg + {\rm Res}_{s=\frac{1}{2}} \int_{\mathcal{D}-\mathcal{D}_T} \varphi(g) \left( {\rm E}(s,f_0)(g) - {\rm E}(s,f_0)_N(g) \right) dg \\
	&\quad + \lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^{(-1)}(0) \int_T^{\infty} (a(t,\varphi)-f(t)) \frac{dt}{t^2},
\end{align*}
	where $\mathcal{D}$ is the standard fundamental domain for $[{\rm PGL}_2]$ and $\mathcal{D}_T$ is the set of $g \in \mathcal{D}$ such that ${\rm Ht}(g) \leq T$.
nodes.statement_short: Residue at $s=1/2$ of the identity in (2).

nodes.name: Vanishing terms
nodes.statement:
It is easy to see that as $T \to \infty$
	$$ h_T(-\frac{1}{2}) \to 0; \quad \int_T^{\infty} (a(t,\varphi)-f(t)) \frac{dt}{t^2} \to 0. $$
nodes.statement_short: Two terms tend to $0$ as $T\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Holomorphy of the tail
nodes.statement:
By Proposition \ref{GlobRDEisWhi}, ${\rm E}(s,f_0)(g) - {\rm E}(s,f_0)_N(g)$ is of uniformly rapid decay with respect to ${\rm Ht}(g), g \in \mathcal{D}$ as $s$ remains in a compact neighborhood of $1/2$. Hence
	$$ \int_{\mathcal{D}-\mathcal{D}_T} \varphi(g) \left( {\rm E}(s,f_0)(g) - {\rm E}(s,f_0)_N(g) \right) dg $$
	is holomorphic at $s=1/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Rapid decay of $E-E_N$ makes the tail integral holomorphic at $1/2$.

nodes.name: Residue of h_T
nodes.statement:
We compute ${\rm Res}_{s=\frac{1}{2}} h_T(s)$ by noting that the second summand of
	$$ \frac{d^n}{d s^n} \left( \frac{T^s}{s} \right) = \frac{(-1)^n n!}{s^{n+1}} + \int_0^{\log T} t^n e^{st} dt $$
is holomorphic at $s=0$, and get
	$$ {\rm Res}_{s=\frac{1}{2}} h_T(s) = c_i \delta_{\substack{\alpha_i=-\frac{1}{2} \\ n_i=0}}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\mathrm{Res}_{s=1/2}h_T(s)$, giving the degenerate term.

nodes.name: Reduction to flat sections
nodes.statement:
Take $f \in {\rm Res}_{\gp{K}}^{{\rm GL}_2(\ag{A})} \pi(\xi, \omega\xi^{-1})$ and the flat section $f_s \in \pi(\xi \norm^s, \omega\xi^{-1} \norm^{-s})$ associated to it. It suffices to show that for any $s_0 \in \ag{C}, n \in \ag{N}$ and fixed $g \in {\rm GL}_2(\ag{A})$, the right translate by $g$ of the partial derivative of this flat section, as a function on ${\rm GL}_2(\ag{A})$
	$$ x \mapsto g.f_{s_0}^{(n)}(x) := \frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} \mid_{s=s_0} f_s(xg) $$
is a linear combination of such functions. The above function is clearly left invariant by $\gp{N}(\ag{A})$, of central character $\omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a flat section and reduce to translates of its $s$-derivatives.

nodes.name: Iwasawa decomposition
nodes.statement:
Taking $x=a(y)\kappa$ for $y \in \ag{A}^{	imes}, \kappa \in \gp{K}$ and writing
	$$ \kappa g = z' n' a(y') \kappa', \quad 	ext{for} \quad z' \in \gp{Z}(\ag{A}), n' \in \gp{N}(\ag{A}), y' \in \ag{A}^{	imes}, \kappa' \in \gp{K}, $$
where $z',n',y',\kappa'$ are viewed as functions in $\kappa$, we obtain
	$$  rac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} \mid_{s=s_0} f_s(a(y)\kappa g) = \sum_{k=0}^n  inom{n}{k} \xi(y) 
orm[y]_{\ag{A}}^{ rac{1}{2}+s_0} (\log 
orm[y]_{\ag{A}})^k \cdot 
orm[y']_{\ag{A}}^{ rac{1}{2}+s_0} (\log 
orm[y']_{\ag{A}})^{n-k} \omega(z') \xi(y') f(\kappa'). $$
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $\kappa g$ and expand the derivative by Leibniz.

nodes.name: Define f_k
nodes.statement:
Although $z',n',y',\kappa'$ are not uniquely determined by $\kappa$, both $
orm[y']_{\ag{A}}$ and $\omega(z') \xi(y') f(\kappa')$ are, and define smooth functions on $\gp{K}$. Moreover, the function
	$$ f_k(\kappa) := 
orm[y']_{\ag{A}}^{ rac{1}{2}+s_0} (\log 
orm[y']_{\ag{A}})^{n-k} \omega(z') \xi(y') f(\kappa') \in {m Res}_{\gp{K}}^{{m GL}_2(\ag{A})} \pi(\xi, \omega\xi^{-1}). $$
nodes.statement_short: The new coefficients $f_k$ are well defined smooth functions on $K$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
Hence we get the relation
	$$ \frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} \mid_{s=s_0} f_s = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} \frac{\partial^k}{\partial s^k} \mid_{s=s_0} f_{k,s} $$
and conclude.
nodes.statement_short: The translate is a combination of derivatives of flat sections.

nodes.name: Setup and basis
nodes.statement: Take a flat section $f_s$ as in the proof of Proposition \ref{FregStab}. Fix $s_0 \in \ag{C}, n \in \ag{N}, g \in {\rm GL}_2(\ag{A})$ with $\Re s_0 > 0$. Let $e_{\vec{k}}$ be an orthonormal $\gp{K}$-isotypic basis of ${\rm Res}_{\gp{K}}^{{\rm GL}_2(\ag{A})} \pi(\xi, \omega\xi^{-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a flat section, $s_0$, $g$ and a $K$-isotypic basis.

nodes.name: Intertwining operator on K-types
nodes.statement:
There is an orthonormal $\gp{K}$-isotypic basis $\tilde{e}_{\vec{k}}$ of ${\rm Res}_{\gp{K}}^{{\rm GL}_2(\ag{A})} \pi(\omega\xi^{-1}, \xi)$ and for any $n \in \ag{N}$ there is $A > 0$ such that (c.f. \cite[\S 3]{Wu5})
	$$ \mathcal{M}_s e_{\vec{k},s} = \mu_{\vec{k}}(s) \tilde{e}_{\vec{k},-s}, \quad \extnorm{\mu_{\vec{k}}^{(n)}(s)} \ll \lambda_{\vec{k}}^A $$
for some meromorphic function $\mu_{\vec{k}}(s)$, regular in $\Re s > 0, s \neq 1/2$. Here $\lambda_{\vec{k}}$ is the eigenvalue of the Laplacian on $\gp{K}_{\infty}$ for $e_{\vec{k}}$, and the bound is uniform for $s$ lying in any  compact subset of the regular region.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal M_s$ acts diagonally on $K$-types with polynomially bounded coefficients (cf. [Wu5]).

nodes.name: Expansion of g.f_s
nodes.statement:
We also have an expansion
	$$ g.f_s = \sideset{}{_{\vec{k}}} \sum a_{\vec{k}}(s,g) e_{\vec{k},s}, $$
for some functions $a_{\vec{k}}(s,g)$ holomorphic in $s$ and smooth in $g$, since
	$$ a_{\vec{k}}(s,g) = \int_{\gp{K}} f_s(\kappa g) \overline{e_{\vec{k}}(\kappa)} d\kappa. $$
	Moreover, we have $ a_{\vec{k}}(s,g) \ll_{g,f,N} \lambda_{\vec{k}}^{-N} $ for any $N \in \ag{N}$, uniformly for $s$ lying in any compact neighborhood of $s_0$. It follows that for any $l \in \ag{N}$
	$$ a_{\vec{k}}^{(l)}(s,g) := \frac{\partial^l}{\partial s^l} \mid_{s=s_0} a_{\vec{k}}(s,g) \ll_{g,f,N} \lambda_{\vec{k}}^{-N}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Expand $g.f_s$ in the basis with rapidly decreasing coefficients.

nodes.name: Derivative expansion
nodes.statement:
We thus get
	$$ g.f_{s_0}^{(n)} = \sideset{}{_{k=0}^n} \sum \sideset{}{_{\vec{k}}} \sum \binom{n}{k} a_{\vec{k}}^{(n-k)}(s_0,g) e_{\vec{k},s_0}^{(k)}. $$
	The inner sum coincides with the value at $s=s_0$ of a flat section $f_{k,s}^{(k)}$ defined by
	$$ f_k = \binom{n}{k} \sideset{}{_{\vec{k}}} \sum a_{\vec{k}}^{(n-k)}(s_0,g) e_{\vec{k}}, $$
which is smooth.
nodes.statement_short: Write $g.f^{(n)}_{s_0}$ via flat sections $f_k$.

nodes.name: Constant terms match
nodes.statement:
We can also verify that
\begin{align*}
	\sideset{}{_{k=0}^n} \sum \frac{\partial^k}{\partial s^k} \mid_{s=s_0} \mathcal{M}_s f_{k,s} &= \sideset{}{_{k=0}^n} \sum \sideset{}{_{\vec{k}}} \sum \binom{n}{k} a_{\vec{k}}^{(n-k)}(s_0,g) \frac{\partial^k}{\partial s^k} \mid_{s=s_0} (\mu_{\vec{k}}(s) \tilde{e}_{\vec{k},-s}) \\
	&= \sideset{}{_{\vec{k}}} \sum \frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} \mid_{s=s_0} (a_{\vec{k}}(s,g) \mu_{\vec{k}}(s) \tilde{e}_{\vec{k},-s}) = \frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} \mid_{s=s_0} \mathcal{M}_s f_s,
\end{align*}
	hence we deduce that
	$$ g.{\rm E}_{\gp{N}}^{(n)}(s_0,f) = \sideset{}{_{k=0}^n} \sum {\rm E}_{\gp{N}}^{(k)}(s_0,f_k). $$
nodes.statement_short: Intertwined parts agree, so constant terms match.

nodes.name: Conclude by cusp-form orthogonality
nodes.statement:
We conclude by
	$$ g.{\rm E}^{(n)}(s_0,f) = \sideset{}{_{k=0}^n} \sum {\rm E}^{(k)}(s_0,f_k) $$
since both sides are orthogonal to the cusp forms and have the same constant term.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides are orthogonal to cusp forms with equal constant terms.

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{IntExpBd} and Proposition \ref{GlobRDEisWhi}, it is not difficult to see that $\mathcal{E}({\rm GL}_2,\omega) \cap {\rm L}^2({\rm GL}_2(\mathbf{F}) \backslash {\rm GL}_2(\ag{A}), \omega) = \{0\}$, which implies the uniqueness of $\mathcal{E}(\varphi)$ in (2).
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal E\cap L^2=\{0\}$ gives uniqueness in (2).

nodes.name: Construct E(phi)
nodes.statement_short: Define $\mathcal E(\varphi)$ by (2.3).

nodes.name: Exponents of the difference
nodes.statement: Thus for any $\chi \in \mathcal{E}{\rm x}(\varphi-\mathcal{E}(\varphi))$, we have $\Re \chi \leq 1/2$ resp. $\Re \chi < 1/2$ under the condition in (2). Hence $\varphi-\mathcal{E}(\varphi) \in {\rm L}^1({\rm GL}_2, \omega)$ resp. ${\rm L}^2({\rm GL}_2, \omega)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi-\mathcal E(\varphi)$ has exponents with $\Re\chi\le1/2$ (resp. $<$), hence is $L^1$ (resp. $L^2$).

nodes.name: Moreover part
nodes.statement:
For the ``moreover'' part, it suffices to see that the differential operator $X$ does not increase the real part of elements in $\mathcal{E}{\rm x}(\varphi)$, which is essentially due to the following calculation:
	$$ y \frac{d}{dy} (y^{\sigma} \log^k y) = y^{\sigma} \log^k y + k y^{\sigma} \log^{k-1}y, \forall y>0, \sigma \in \ag{C}, k \in \ag{N}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Differential operators do not increase real parts of exponents.

nodes.name: Reduce second assertion
nodes.statement: For (1), the second assertion follows from the first by Proposition \ref{Reis+Stab}.
nodes.statement_short: Second assertion of (1) from the first by Proposition 2.21.

nodes.name: Generators of residual space
nodes.statement: We calculate $a(t,\mathcal{E})$ for $\mathcal{E}(g) = \frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} {\rm E}(s,f)(gg_0)$ with $s \neq 1/2-i\mu(\chi)$ resp. $\frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} {\rm E}^{{\rm reg}}(\frac{1}{2}-i\mu(\chi),f)(g)$ for some $f \in V_{\chi,\chi^{-1}}^{\infty}$ with $\Re s > 0$, a unitary character $\chi$ of $\mathbf{F}^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}^{\times}$ if $\chi \mid_{\mathbf{F}^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}^{(1)}} = 1$. Due to the integral $\int_{\mathbf{F}^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}^{(1)}} d^{\times}y$, it is easy to see that $a(t,\varphi)$ is non-vanishing only if $\chi$ is trivial on $\mathbf{F}^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}^{(1)}$, in which case $\mu(\omega\chi^2)=2\mu(\chi)$. We also notice that we can interchange the order of $\mathcal{M}$ and $\int_{\gp{K}} dk$ since they commute with each other.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the kernel $a(t,\mathcal E)$ for the generators; only characters trivial on $\mathbb A^{(1)}$ contribute.

nodes.name: Case of Eisenstein series
nodes.statement:
$\mathcal{E}(g) = \frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} {\rm E}(s,f)(g)$ with $s \neq 1/2-i\mu(\chi)$: We get
	$$ a(t,\mathcal{E}) = \zeta_{\mathbf{F}}^*(1) \int_{\gp{K}} f(k)dk \cdot \left\{ t^{\frac{1}{2}+s+i\mu(\chi)} \log^n t + \frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} \left( t^{\frac{1}{2}-s-i\mu(\chi)} \frac{\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(1-2s-2i\mu(\chi))}{\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(1+2s+2i\mu(\chi))} \right) \right\}, $$
	and conclude by the fact that $a(t,\mathcal{E})$ has no constant term as a function of $t$.
nodes.statement_short: $a(t,\mathcal E)$ has no constant term.

nodes.name: Case of regularizing Eisenstein series
nodes.statement:
$\mathcal{E}(g)=\frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} {\rm E}^{{\rm reg}}(\frac{1}{2}-i\mu(\chi),f)(g)$: We get
\begin{align*}
	a(t,\mathcal{E}) &= \zeta_{\mathbf{F}}^*(1) \int_{\gp{K}} f(k)dk \cdot \\
	&\quad \left\{ t \log^n t + \frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} \mid_{s=\frac{1}{2}-i\mu(\chi)} \left( (t^{\frac{1}{2}-s-i\mu(\chi)}-1) \frac{\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(1-2s-2i\mu(\chi))}{\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(1+2s+2i\mu(\chi))} \right) \right\} \\
	&= \zeta_{\mathbf{F}}^*(1) \int_{\gp{K}} f(k)dk \cdot \\
	&\quad \left\{ t \log^n t + \sum_{l=0}^n \binom{n}{l} \frac{(-1)^l}{l+1} \cdot \log^{l+1}t \cdot \frac{d^{n-l}}{d s^{n-l}} \mid_{s=0} \left( \frac{s\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(2s)}{\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(2-2s)} \right) \right\},
\end{align*}
	and conclude the same way as in the previous case.
nodes.statement_short: Same conclusion for $E^{reg}$.

nodes.name: Part (2)
nodes.statement: For (2), the first part is trivial. For the second part, we note that $\varphi-\mathcal{E}(\varphi) \in {\rm L}^1$ implies $g_0.\varphi-g_0.\mathcal{E}(\varphi) \in {\rm L}^1$ for any $g_0 \in {\rm GL}_2(\ag{A})$, and $g_0.\mathcal{E}(\varphi)$ has regularized integral $0$ by (1) if either $\mathcal{E} \in \mathcal{E}^+({\rm GL}_2,1)$ or $g_0 \in \gp{K}$.
nodes.statement_short: Translate $\varphi-\mathcal E$ and use (1).

nodes.name: R as product of L-functions
nodes.statement:
$R(s, {\rm E}^{(n_1)}(0,f_1) {\rm E}^{(n_2)}(0,f_2))$ resp. $R(s, {\rm E}^{\sharp,(n_1)}(1/2,f_1) {\rm E}^{\sharp,(n_2)}(1/2,f_2))$ represents the value at $s_1=s_2=0$ of $\partial_1^{n_1} \partial_2^{n_2}$ of
	$$ \Lambda(1/2+s+s_1+s_2, \xi_1\xi_2) \Lambda(1/2+s+s_1-s_2, \xi_1\xi_2') \Lambda(1/2+s-s_1+s_2, \xi_1'\xi_2) \Lambda(1/2+s-s_1-s_2, \xi_1'\xi_2') \quad \text{resp.} $$
	$$ \Lambda(3/2+s+s_1+s_2, \xi_1\xi_2) \Lambda(1/2+s+s_1-s_2, \xi_1\xi_2') \Lambda(1/2+s-s_1+s_2, \xi_1'\xi_2) \Lambda(-1/2+s-s_1-s_2, \xi_1'\xi_2'), $$
which is regular at $s=1/2$ by assumption. The degenerate part is also easily seen to be $0$ by assumption.
nodes.statement_short: $R(s,\cdot)$ is a product of completed $L$-functions regular at $1/2$; the degenerate part vanishes.

nodes.name: Apply definition
nodes.statement: We conclude by Definition \ref{RegIntDef}.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude from Definition 2.12.

nodes.name: Similar to Theorem 2.11
nodes.statement: The proof is quite similar to that of Theorem \ref{AdelicRegThm} (3), except that $\mathcal{M} f_s$ is no longer explicitly computable.
nodes.statement_short: Follow Theorem 2.11(3).

nodes.name: Unfolding
nodes.statement:
In fact, we have for $T > 1, \Re s \gg 1$, using the standard Rankin-Selberg unfolding
\begin{align*}
	\int_{[{\rm PGL}_2]} \varphi \cdot \Lambda^T {\rm E}(s,f) &= R(s,\varphi; f) \\
	&- \int_{\mathbf{F}^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}^{\times}} \left( \int_{\gp{K}} (\varphi_{\gp{N}} - \varphi_{\gp{N}}^*)(a(y)\kappa) f(\kappa) d\kappa \right) \xi_1(y) \norm[y]_{\ag{A}}^{s-1/2} 1_{\norm[y]_{\ag{A}} > T} d^{\times} y \\
	&- \int_{\mathbf{F}^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}^{\times}} \left( \int_{\gp{K}} (\varphi_{\gp{N}} - \varphi_{\gp{N}}^*)(a(y)\kappa) \mathcal{M} f_s(\kappa) d\kappa \right) \xi_2(y) \norm[y]_{\ag{A}}^{-s-1/2} 1_{\norm[y]_{\ag{A}} > T} d^{\times} y \\
	&+ {\rm Vol}(\mathbf{F}^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}^{(1)}) \left( \sum_{j=1}^l \int_{\gp{K}} f_j(\kappa) f(\kappa) d\kappa \cdot 1_{\chi_j \xi_1(\ag{A}^{(1)}) = 1} \cdot \frac{1}{n_j !} \frac{\partial^{n_j}}{\partial s^{n_j}} \left( \frac{T^{s+\alpha_j + i\mu_j}}{s+\alpha_j + i\mu_j} \right) \right. \\
	&- \left. \sum_{j=1}^l \int_{\gp{K}} f_j(\kappa) \mathcal{M} f_s(\kappa) d\kappa \cdot 1_{\chi_j \xi_2(\ag{A}^{(1)}) = 1} \cdot \frac{(-1)^{n_j}}{n_j !} \frac{\partial^{n_j}}{\partial s^{n_j}} \left( \frac{T^{-s+\alpha_j + i\mu_j'}}{-s+\alpha_j + i\mu_j'} \right) \right),
\end{align*}
where $\mu_j$ resp. $\mu_j'$ is such that
	$$ \chi_j \xi_1(y) = \norm[y]_{\ag{A}}^{i\mu_j}, \quad \text{resp.} \quad \chi_j \xi_2(y) = \norm[y]_{\ag{A}}^{i\mu_j'}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Unfold $\int\varphi\Lambda^TE(s,f)$.

nodes.name: Shift and limit
nodes.statement: We conclude by first shifting $s$ to the desired region, then letting $T \to \infty$. The possible poles are encoded in the possible poles of $\mathcal{M} f_s$, which are included in those of $L(1+2s, \xi_1\xi_2^{-1})^{-1}$ in the above region (c.f. for example \cite[Corollary 3.7, 3.10 \& Lemma 3.18]{Wu5}).
nodes.statement_short: Shift $s$, let $T\to\infty$; poles come from $\mathcal Mf_s$.

nodes.name: Reduce to xi = 1
nodes.statement: The case (1) being simpler, we only give details for (2). By twisting, we may assume $\xi=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Treat (2) only and twist to $\xi=1$.

nodes.name: L^2-residue of the product
nodes.statement:
Let $s$ be small with $\Re s < 0$. The ${\rm L}^2$-residue of $\varphi \cdot {\rm E}(1/2+s,f)$ is given by
	$$ \mathcal{E}(s) := \sideset{}{_j} \sum {\rm E}^{(n_j)}(s+1+\alpha_j, f_j f), $$
	where the summation is over $j$ such that $\Re \alpha_j > -1$.
nodes.statement_short: Write the $L^2$-residue $\mathcal E(s)$ of $\varphi E(1/2+s,f)$.

nodes.name: Regularized residue
nodes.statement:
Define
	$$ \mathcal{E}^{{\rm reg}}(s) := \sideset{}{_j'} \sum {\rm E}^{{\rm reg},(n_j)}(s+1+\alpha_j, f_j f) + \sideset{}{_j^*} \sum {\rm E}^{(n_j)}(s+1+\alpha_j, f_j f) $$
where $\sideset{}{_j'} \sum$ is the summation as in the statement and $\sideset{}{_j^*} \sum$ is the rest.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\mathcal E^{reg}(s)$.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 4.1
nodes.statement_short: Express $R(1/2+s,\varphi;f)$ through the regularized pieces.

nodes.name: Compare holomorphic parts
nodes.statement:
Since $\mathcal{E}^{{\rm reg},(n)}(s)$ is the ${\rm L}^2$-residue of $\varphi \cdot {\rm E}^{{\rm reg},(n)}(\frac{1}{2}+s,f)$, we can compare the holomorphic part of both sides and conclude by
	$$ \mathcal{E}(s) - \mathcal{E}^{{\rm reg}}(s) = \sideset{}{_j'} \sum \lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^{(n_j)}(s) {\rm P}_{\gp{K}}(f_jf). $$
nodes.statement_short: Compare holomorphic parts at $s=0$.

nodes.name: Sketch only
nodes.statement: We shall only point out how the computation is effectuated, since the formulas are quite long.
nodes.statement_short: Only the structure of the computation is given.

nodes.name: Split off the L^2-residue
nodes.statement_short: Subtract the $L^2$-residue $\mathcal E(f_1,f_2)$ of $E^*E^*$ and split the integral in two.

nodes.name: First term
nodes.statement:
The first term is computed by Proposition \ref{TripleToDouble} (2), involving
	$$ \int_{[{\rm PGL}_2]} \varphi = \int_{[{\rm PGL}_2]}^{{\rm reg}} {\rm E}^*(0,f_1) \cdot {\rm E}^*(0,f_2) = \frac{(\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^*)^2}{4} \int_{[{\rm PGL}_2]}^{{\rm reg}} {\rm E}^{(1)}(0,f_1) \cdot {\rm E}^{(1)}(0,f_2), $$
which is treated in Theorem \ref{RIPEisUnitary} (2).
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 4.2(2) and Theorem 3.4(2).

nodes.name: Second term
nodes.statement: The second term is treated in Theorem \ref{RIPEisSing} (3).
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 3.7(3).

nodes.name: L^l by sup norms
nodes.statement:
In the case $d=1$, we have for $l \in [1,\infty)$ and any $\Phi \in \mathcal{S}(\ag{R})$
	$$ \int_{\ag{R}} \norm[\Phi(x)]^l dx \leq \mathcal{S}_{\infty}^{0,0}(\Phi)^l \int_{-1}^1 dx + \mathcal{S}_{\infty}^{2,0}(\Phi)^l \int_{\norm[x]>1} \norm[x]^{-2l} dx, $$
from which we deduce by replacing $\Phi(x)$ with $x^p \Phi^{(m)}(x)$ that
	$$ \mathcal{S}_l^{p,m}(\Phi) \ll_l \mathcal{S}_{\infty}^{p,m}(\Phi) + \mathcal{S}_{\infty}^{p+2,m}(\Phi). $$
nodes.statement_short: Bound $L^l$ semi-norms by sup semi-norms for $d=1$.

nodes.name: Hölder estimate
nodes.statement:
In the opposite direction, from H"older inequality
	$$ 
orm[\Phi(y) - \Phi(x)] = \extnorm{ \int_x^y \Phi'(t) dt} \leq \Norm[\Phi']_l \cdot \left( \int_x^y dt ight)^{ rac{1-l}{l}} $$
and $(a+b)^l \leq 2^{l-1}(a^l + b^l)$ we deduce
	$$ 
orm[\Phi(y)]^l \leq 2^{l-1} \left( 
orm[\Phi(x)]^l + \Norm[\Phi']_l^l \cdot 
orm[y-x]^{l-1} ight). $$
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise estimate via Hölder.

nodes.name: Sobolev inequality
nodes.statement:
Integrating both sides against $\min(1,
orm[x-y]^{-l-1})dx \leq dx$ gives
	$$ (2+ rac{2}{l}) 
orm[\Phi(y)]^l \leq 2^{l-1} \left( \Norm[\Phi]_l^l + \Norm[\Phi']_l^l \cdot \int_{\ag{R}} \min(
orm[x]^{l-1}, 
orm[x]^{-2}) dx ight). $$
	Hence we get (a Sobolev inequality) and conclude the case $d=1$ by
	$$ \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty} \ll_l \Norm[\Phi]_l + \Norm[\Phi']_l. $$
nodes.statement_short: Average to get a Sobolev inequality, finishing $d=1$.

nodes.name: Induction on d
nodes.statement:
For general $d$, one deduces easily by induction
	$$ \mathcal{S}_l^{\vec{p},\vec{m}}(\Phi)^l \ll_{l,d} \sum_{\vec{\epsilon} \in \{ 0,2 \}^d} \mathcal{S}_{\infty}^{\vec{p}+\vec{\epsilon},\vec{m}}(\Phi)^l, $$
	$$ \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}^l \ll_{l,d} \sum_{\vec{\epsilon} \in \{ 0,1 \}^d} \mathcal{S}_l^{0,\vec{\epsilon}}(\Phi)^l. $$
nodes.statement_short: Induct on the dimension.

nodes.name: Reduce to uniform continuity
nodes.statement:
{(of Lemma \ref{SchNormEquivA})}
	By the above proposition, the problem is reduced to the uniform continuity of
	$$ \Four[2]{\cdot} \circ {\rm R}(\kappa): \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{F}^2) \to \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{F}^2) $$
with respect to $\kappa \in \gp{K}$.
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 5.8 reduce to uniform continuity of $\mathfrak F_2\circ R(\kappa)$.

nodes.name: Check continuity
nodes.statement: The continuity of $\Four[2]{\cdot}$ follows by considering the $\mathcal{S}_2^*$ semi-norms. The uniform continuity of ${\rm R}(\kappa)$ follows by considering the $\mathcal{S}_{\infty}^*$ semi-norms.
nodes.statement_short: Use $\mathcal S_2$ and $\mathcal S_\infty$ semi-norms.

nodes.name: First inequality
nodes.statement:
The first inequality follows from
	$$ \int_0^{\infty} \norm[f^{(k)}(y) y^{\sigma+k}]^l \frac{dy}{y} \leq B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma + \epsilon}(f)^l \int_1^{\infty} y^{-\epsilon l} \frac{dy}{y} + B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma - \epsilon}(f)^l \int_0^1 y^{\epsilon l} \frac{dy}{y}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Split the integral at $y=1$.

nodes.name: Integral identity
nodes.statement:
For the second inequality, we first note that for any $x,y > 0$
	$$ f^{(k)}(y)y^{\sigma+k} - f^{(k)}(x)x^{\sigma+k} = \int_y^x f^{(k+1)}(u) u^{\sigma+k+1} \frac{du}{u} + (\sigma + k) \int_y^x f^{(k)}(u) u^{\sigma+k} \frac{du}{u}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Write the difference of values as an integral.

nodes.name: Hölder bound
nodes.statement:
We can bound the integrals using H"older inequality as
	$$ \extnorm{\int_y^x f^{(k)}(u) u^{\sigma+k}  rac{du}{u}} \leq B_l^{k,\sigma}(f) \cdot 
orm[\log (y/x)]^{ rac{l-1}{l}}, $$
from which we deduce
	$$ 
orm[f^{(k)}(y)y^{\sigma+k}] \leq 
orm[f^{(k)}(x)x^{\sigma+k}] + \left[ B_l^{k+1,\sigma}(f) + 
orm[\sigma+k] \cdot B_l^{k,\sigma}(f) ight] \cdot 
orm[\log (y/x)]^{ rac{l-1}{l}}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Bound the integrals with Hölder.

nodes.name: Average
nodes.statement:
Raising to the power $l \geq 1$ and use $(a+b)^l \leq 2^{l-1}(a^l + b^l)$ gives
	$$ 
orm[f^{(k)}(y)y^{\sigma+k}]^l \leq 2^{l-1} \left\{ 
orm[f^{(k)}(x)x^{\sigma+k}]^l + \left[ B_l^{k+1,\sigma}(f) + 
orm[\sigma+k] \cdot B_l^{k,\sigma}(f) ight]^l \cdot 
orm[\log (y/x)]^{l-1} ight\}. $$
	Integrating both sides against $\min((x/y)^{\epsilon l}, (x/y)^{-\epsilon l}) dx/x \leq dx/x$ gives
	$$  rac{2}{\epsilon l} \cdot 
orm[f^{(k)}(y)y^{\sigma+k}]^l \leq 2^{l-1} \left\{ B_l^{k,\sigma}(f)^l + \left[ B_l^{k+1,\sigma}(f) + 
orm[\sigma+k] \cdot B_l^{k,\sigma}(f) ight]^l \cdot \int_0^{\infty} \min(x^{\epsilon},x^{-\epsilon}) 
orm[\log x]^{l-1}  rac{dx}{x} ight\}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Raise to the $l$-th power and integrate against a kernel.

nodes.name: Finite kernel integral
nodes.statement: We conclude since $\int_0^{\infty} \min(x^{\epsilon},x^{-\epsilon}) \norm[\log x]^{l-1} \frac{dx}{x} < \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: The kernel integral is finite.

nodes.name: First inequality
nodes.statement_short: Split the line at $|\Im s|=1$.

nodes.name: Cauchy formula
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy's formula on two shifted lines.

nodes.name: Hölder
nodes.statement_short: Bound each line integral by Hölder.

nodes.name: Real case
nodes.statement:
In the case $\mathbf{F}=\ag{R}$, we have
	$$ t^k\frac{d^k}{dt^k} f(t;+) = \frac{1}{2} \left( t^kf^{(k)}(t) + (-1)^k t^k f^{(k)}(-t) \right), $$
	$$ t^k\frac{d^k}{dt^k} f(t;-) = \frac{1}{2} \left( t^kf^{(k)}(t) + (-1)^{k+1} t^k f^{(k)}(-t) \right), $$
from which it is easy to see
	$$ B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(f_{\pm}) \leq \mathcal{S}_{\infty}^{\lfloor k+\sigma \rfloor, k}(f) + \mathcal{S}_{\infty}^{\lceil k+\sigma \rceil, k}(f), \forall k \in \ag{N}, \sigma > 0. $$
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate $f_\pm$ directly.

nodes.name: Complex case
nodes.statement:
In the case $\mathbf{F}=\ag{C}$, with the Cartesian \& Polar coordinates
	$$ (x,y) = (t \cos \theta, t \sin \theta), (z,\bar{z})=(x+iy,x-iy) $$
	we have
	$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} = i \left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} - \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}} \right); t\frac{\partial}{\partial t} = z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}}. $$
	By induction on $k \in \ag{N}$, it is easy to see
	$$ t^k \frac{\partial^k}{\partial t^k} = P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}}) $$
for some polynomial $P_k \in \ag{Z}[X]$ and any $k \in \ag{N}$. It follows that
\begin{align*}
	t^k f_n^{(k)}(t) &= \int_{\ag{R} / 2\pi \ag{Z}} (P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}})f)(te^{i\theta}) e^{in\theta} \frac{d\theta}{2\pi} \\
	&= \frac{(-1)^l}{n^l} \int_{\ag{R} / 2\pi \ag{Z}} (\left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} - \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}} \right)^l P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}})f)(te^{i\theta}) e^{in\theta} \frac{d\theta}{2\pi}.
\end{align*}
	Hence, we deduce that
\begin{align*}
	B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(f_n) &\leq \norm[n]^{-l} \left\{ \extNorm{(z\bar{z})^{\lfloor \frac{\sigma}{2} \rfloor}\left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} - \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}} \right)^l P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}})f}_{\infty} \right. \\
	&\quad \left. + \extNorm{(z\bar{z})^{\lceil \frac{\sigma}{2} \rceil}\left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} - \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}} \right)^l P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}})f}_{\infty} \right\}.
\end{align*}
	The right hand side is obviously bounded by some Schwartz norm of $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Polar coordinates and integration by parts in $\theta$.

nodes.name: Polar coordinates
nodes.statement:
In the case $\mathbf{F}=\ag{C}$, with the Cartesian \& Polar coordinates
	$$ (x,y) = (t \cos \theta, t \sin \theta), (z,\bar{z})=(x+iy,x-iy) $$
	we have
	$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} = i \left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} - \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}} \right); t\frac{\partial}{\partial t} = z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Express $\partial_\theta$ and $t\partial_t$ through $z\partial_z,\bar z\partial_{\bar z}$.

nodes.name: Polynomial in Euler operators
nodes.statement:
By induction on $k \in \ag{N}$, it is easy to see
	$$ t^k \frac{\partial^k}{\partial t^k} = P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}}) $$
for some polynomial $P_k \in \ag{Z}[X]$ and any $k \in \ag{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: $t^k\partial_t^k$ is a polynomial in $t\partial_t$.

nodes.name: Integrate by parts and bound
nodes.statement_short: Integrate by parts $l$ times in $\theta$ and bound by Schwartz norms.

nodes.name: Complex case only
nodes.statement:
{(of Lemma \ref{IntBdA})}
	We only treat the case $\mathbf{F}=\ag{C}$, the real case being similar and simpler.
nodes.statement_short: Treat $\mathbf F=\mathbb C$.

nodes.name: Angular Fourier expansion
nodes.statement:
Writing
	$$ f(y) = \int_{\ag{C}^{\times}} \Phi(t,\frac{y}{t}) \omega^{-1}\xi^2(t)\norm[t]_{\ag{C}}^{2s} d^{\times}t, $$
we can take its Fourier expansion on $\ag{C}^1$
	$$ f(te^{i\theta}) = \sum_{n \in \ag{Z}} f_n(t) e^{-in\theta}, t \in \ag{R}_+. $$
nodes.statement_short: Expand $f$ in angular Fourier series.

nodes.name: Mellin transform of components
nodes.statement_short: Compute the Mellin transform of $f_n$ as a two-variable Mellin transform of $\Phi$.

nodes.name: Bound in H-norms
nodes.statement:
Considering the $H_{\infty}^*$ semi-norms it is easy to see $\Mellin{f_n} \in {\rm H}_{\max(0,-4\Re s)}(\ag{C})$. We can also bound
	$$ H_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(\Mellin{f_n}) \ll_{k,\sigma} \min(1, \norm[n]^{-2}) \mathcal{S}_1^*(\Phi), \forall \sigma > \max(0,-4\Re s). $$
	As $\Re s$ lies in a compact interval, the orders of $\mathcal{S}_1^*$ can be made uniform (but depends on $\sigma$).
nodes.statement_short: Bound $H_\infty$ semi-norms of $\mathfrak M f_n$ uniformly with decay in $n$.

nodes.name: Sum over n
nodes.statement:
Hence $f_n \in {m B}_{\max(0,-4\Re s)}(\ag{R}_+)$ and for any $\sigma > \max(0,-4\Re s)$ we get
	$$ 
orm[t^{\sigma}f(te^{i	heta})] \leq \sum_n B_{\infty}^{0,\sigma}(f_n) \ll \mathcal{S}_1^*(\Phi) \sum_n \min(1, 
orm[n]^{-2}). $$
	We conclude by noting $t^{\sigma} = 
orm[te^{i	heta}]_{\ag{C}}^{\sigma/2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Invert and sum over $n$.

nodes.name: Parts (0) and (1)
nodes.statement: (0) and (1) are obvious from definition.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definitions.

nodes.name: Part (3) from (2)
nodes.statement: (3) follows easily from (2).
nodes.statement_short: (3) reduces to (2).

nodes.name: Proof of (2)
nodes.statement:
We prove (2) as follows. From
	$$ \Four{\Phi}(\vec{x}+\vec{t}) = \int_{\mathfrak{p}^{D(\Phi)} \times \cdots \times \mathfrak{p}^{D(\Phi)}} \Phi(\vec{y}) \psi(-\vec{y}.\vec{x}) \psi(-\vec{y}.\vec{t}) d\vec{y}, $$
we see that for $\vec{t} \in \mathfrak{p}^{-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-D(\Phi)}$, $\vec{y}.\vec{t} \in \mathfrak{p}^{-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)}$ hence $\psi(-\vec{y}.\vec{t})=1$ and $\Four{\Phi}(\vec{x}+\vec{t}) = \Four{\Phi}(\vec{x})$. Thus
	$$ \delta(\Four{\Phi}) \leq -\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-D(\Phi). $$
	On the other hand, if $\vec{x} \notin \mathfrak{p}^{-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-\delta(\Phi)} \times \cdots \times \mathfrak{p}^{-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-\delta(\Phi)}$ then at least for one component, say $x_1 \notin \mathfrak{p}^{-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-\delta(\Phi)}$, i.e., $v(x_1) < -\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-\delta(\Phi)$. As $t_1$ runs under the condition $v(t_1)=-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-1-v(x_1) \geq \delta(\Phi)$, $x_1t_1$ runs under the condition $v(x_1t_1)=-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-1$. Hence at least for one $t_1$, $\psi(x_1t_1) \neq 1$. Writing $\vec{t}=(t_1,0,\dots,0)$, we get
	$$ \Four{\Phi}(\vec{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{F}^d} \Phi(\vec{y}+\vec{t}) \psi(-\vec{y}.\vec{x}) d\vec{y} = \int_{\mathbf{F}^d} \Phi(\vec{y}) \psi(-\vec{y}.\vec{x}) d\vec{y} \cdot \psi(\vec{t}.\vec{x}) = \psi(t_1x_1) \Four{\Phi}(\vec{x}). $$
	Hence $\Four{\Phi}(\vec{x}) = 0$ and
	$$ D(\Four{\Phi}) \geq -\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-\delta(\Phi). $$
	Replacing $\Phi$ with $\Four{\Phi}$ in the above argument gives the inequalities in the opposite direction.
nodes.statement_short: Bound invariance and support of the Fourier transform.

nodes.name: Invariance of the Fourier transform
nodes.statement:
We prove (2) as follows. From
	$$ \Four{\Phi}(\vec{x}+\vec{t}) = \int_{\mathfrak{p}^{D(\Phi)} \times \cdots \times \mathfrak{p}^{D(\Phi)}} \Phi(\vec{y}) \psi(-\vec{y}.\vec{x}) \psi(-\vec{y}.\vec{t}) d\vec{y}, $$
we see that for $\vec{t} \in \mathfrak{p}^{-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-D(\Phi)}$, $\vec{y}.\vec{t} \in \mathfrak{p}^{-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)}$ hence $\psi(-\vec{y}.\vec{t})=1$ and $\Four{\Phi}(\vec{x}+\vec{t}) = \Four{\Phi}(\vec{x})$. Thus
	$$ \delta(\Four{\Phi}) \leq -\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-D(\Phi). $$
nodes.statement_short: $\delta(\mathfrak F\Phi)\le-\mathfrak c(\psi)-D(\Phi)$.

nodes.name: Support of the Fourier transform
nodes.statement:
On the other hand, if $\vec{x} \notin \mathfrak{p}^{-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-\delta(\Phi)} \times \cdots \times \mathfrak{p}^{-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-\delta(\Phi)}$ then at least for one component, say $x_1 \notin \mathfrak{p}^{-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-\delta(\Phi)}$, i.e., $v(x_1) < -\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-\delta(\Phi)$. As $t_1$ runs under the condition $v(t_1)=-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-1-v(x_1) \geq \delta(\Phi)$, $x_1t_1$ runs under the condition $v(x_1t_1)=-\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-1$. Hence at least for one $t_1$, $\psi(x_1t_1) \neq 1$. Writing $\vec{t}=(t_1,0,\dots,0)$, we get
	$$ \Four{\Phi}(\vec{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{F}^d} \Phi(\vec{y}+\vec{t}) \psi(-\vec{y}.\vec{x}) d\vec{y} = \int_{\mathbf{F}^d} \Phi(\vec{y}) \psi(-\vec{y}.\vec{x}) d\vec{y} \cdot \psi(\vec{t}.\vec{x}) = \psi(t_1x_1) \Four{\Phi}(\vec{x}). $$
	Hence $\Four{\Phi}(\vec{x}) = 0$ and
	$$ D(\Four{\Phi}) \geq -\mathfrak{c}(\psi)-\delta(\Phi). $$
nodes.statement_short: $D(\mathfrak F\Phi)\ge-\mathfrak c(\psi)-\delta(\Phi)$ via a character that is non-trivial.

nodes.name: Reverse inequalities
nodes.statement: Replacing $\Phi$ with $\Four{\Phi}$ in the above argument gives the inequalities in the opposite direction.
nodes.statement_short: Apply to $\mathfrak F\Phi$ for the opposite inequalities.

nodes.name: Reduce to d = 1
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove the case $d=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $d=1$.

nodes.name: First inequality
nodes.statement:
Let $x_0 \in \mathbf{F}$ be such that $\norm[\Phi(x_0)] = \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}$, then
	$$ \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}^l = {\rm Vol}(\mathfrak{p}^{\delta(\Phi)})^{-1} \int_{x_0 + \mathfrak{p}^{\delta(\Phi)}} \norm[\Phi(x)]^l dx \leq q^{\delta(\Phi)} \Norm[\Phi]_l^l $$
and we get the first inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Average over a ball of invariance around a maximum point.

nodes.name: Second inequality
nodes.statement:
The second follows from
	$$ \Norm[\Phi]_l^l \leq \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}^l \int_{{\rm supp}(\Phi)} dx \leq \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}^l \cdot {\rm Vol}(\mathfrak{p}^{D(\Phi)}) = q^{-D(\Phi)} \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}^l. $$
nodes.statement_short: Bound by the volume of the support.

nodes.name: Weighted norm
nodes.statement_short: Bound the weight on the support.

nodes.name: Fix s_0
nodes.statement: The first is obvious. For the second, let $s_0$ be any complex number with $\Re s_0 = \sigma$ and $0 < \Im s_0 < 2\pi / \log q$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $s_0$ on the line $\Re s=\sigma$.

nodes.name: Cauchy formula
nodes.statement:
Selecting the contour joining $\sigma+\epsilon$, $\sigma+\epsilon + i 2\pi / \log q$, $\sigma - \epsilon + i 2\pi / \log q$ and $\sigma-\epsilon$, we see
	$$ \log q \cdot M(s_0) = \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} \frac{M(\sigma+\epsilon+i\tau)}{\sigma+\epsilon+i\tau - s_0} \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi} - \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} \frac{M(\sigma-\epsilon+i\tau)}{\sigma-\epsilon+i\tau - s_0} \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy's formula on the period rectangle.

nodes.name: Hölder
nodes.statement_short: Bound by $H_l$ norms.

nodes.name: Take sup
nodes.statement: We conclude by taking $\sup$ with respect to $\Re s_0 = \sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the sup over $s_0$.

nodes.name: Mellin transform of components
nodes.statement:
Writing
	$$ f(y) = \int_{\mathbf{F}^{\times}} \Phi(t,\frac{y}{t}) \omega^{-1}\xi^2(t)\norm[t]_{\mathbf{F}}^{2s} d^{\times}t, $$
we have for any $\xi_1 \in \widehat{\mathbf{F}^1}$ and $s_1 \in \ag{C}$ with $\Re s_1 > \max(0,-2\Re s)$
\begin{align*}
	\Mellin{f_{\xi_1}}(s_1) &= \int_{\mathbf{F}^{\times} \times \mathbf{F}^{\times}} \Phi(t,y) \omega^{-1}\xi^2\xi_1(t) \norm[t]_{\mathbf{F}}^{s_1+2s} \xi_1(y) \norm[y]_{\mathbf{F}}^{s_1} d^{\times}t d^{\times}y \\
	&= \Mellin{\Phi_{\omega^{-1}\xi^2\xi_1, \xi_1}}(s_1+2s+i\mu(\omega^{-1}\xi^2), s_1),
\end{align*}
where the second Mellin transform is the natural two dimensional one.
nodes.statement_short: Mellin transform of $f_{\xi_1}$ is a two-variable Mellin transform of $\Phi$.

nodes.name: Finitely many characters
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{SchToB}, $\Phi_{\omega^{-1}\xi^2\xi_1, \xi_1} \neq 0$ only if $\mathfrak{c}(\omega^{-1}\xi^2\xi_1), \mathfrak{c}(\xi_1) \leq m(\Phi)$. In particular, the number of such $\xi_1$ is bounded by $q^{m(\Phi)}$.
nodes.statement_short: At most $q^{m(\Phi)}$ characters contribute.

nodes.name: Chain of norm estimates
nodes.statement:
From the Mellin inversion for $\sigma > \max(0,-2\Re s)$
	$$ f(\varpi^n u) = \sum_{\xi_1} f_{\xi_1}(\varpi^n) \xi_1(u)^{-1} = \sum_{\xi_1} \xi_1(u)^{-1} \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} \Mellin{f_{\xi_1}}(\sigma+i\tau) q^{n(\sigma+i\tau)} \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi} $$
we can successively apply Proposition \ref{HEquiv}, \ref{BHEquiv}, \ref{BEquiv}, \ref{SchToB} and \ref{SchEquiv} to get
\begin{align*}
	\norm[y]_{\mathbf{F}}^{\sigma} \norm[f(y)] &\leq \sum_{\xi_1} H_1^{\sigma}(\Mellin{f_{\xi_1}}) \leq \sum_{\xi_1} H_{\infty}^{\sigma}(\Mellin{f_{\xi_1}}) \\
	&\leq \sum_{\xi_1} H_{\infty}^{\sigma+2\Re s, \sigma}(\Mellin{\Phi_{\omega^{-1}\xi^2\xi_1, \xi_1}}) \leq \sum_{\xi_1}  B_1^{\sigma+2\Re s, \sigma}(\Phi_{\omega^{-1}\xi^2\xi_1, \xi_1})  \\
	&\ll_{\epsilon} \sum_{\xi_1}  \left( B_{\infty}^{\sigma+2\Re s+\epsilon, \sigma+\epsilon} +B_{\infty}^{\sigma+2\Re s+\epsilon, \sigma-\epsilon} + B_{\infty}^{\sigma+2\Re s-\epsilon, \sigma+\epsilon} +B_{\infty}^{\sigma+2\Re s-\epsilon, \sigma-\epsilon} \right)(\Phi_{\omega^{-1}\xi^2\xi_1, \xi_1}) \\
	&\leq \left( \mathcal{S}_{\infty}^{\sigma+2\Re s+\epsilon, \sigma+\epsilon} + \mathcal{S}_{\infty}^{\sigma+2\Re s+\epsilon, \sigma-\epsilon} + \mathcal{S}_{\infty}^{\sigma+2\Re s-\epsilon, \sigma+\epsilon} + \mathcal{S}_{\infty}^{\sigma+2\Re s-\epsilon, \sigma-\epsilon} \right)(\Phi) \sum_{\xi_1}1 \\
	&\leq q^{-ND(\Phi)+m(\Phi)} \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}.
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Mellin inversion and Propositions 5.25, 5.26, 5.24, 5.27, 5.19.

nodes.name: Support
nodes.statement: Finally, it is obvious that $f(y) \neq 0$ implies the existence of some $t \in \mathbf{F}^{\times}$ such that $(t,y/t)$ lies in the support of $\Phi$ hence in $\mathfrak{p}^{D(\Phi)} \times \mathfrak{p}^{D(\Phi)}$, thus $y \in \mathfrak{p}^{2D(\Phi)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Support of $\Phi$ gives $y\in\mathfrak p^{2D(\Phi)}$.

nodes.name: Growth vs decay
nodes.statement: The lemma shows that $(s-s_0)^n \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n})$ is polynomially increasing in $\vec{n}$. But $\hat{f}_{\vec{n}}$ is rapidly decreasing in $\vec{n}$ by smoothness of $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Polynomial growth of $\mu$ (Lemma 5.32) against rapid decay of $\hat f_{\vec n}$.

nodes.name: Uniform convergence
nodes.statement: The sum over $\vec{n}$ is thus absolutely and uniformly convergent for $s$ lying in $K$, hence defines an analytic function in $s$.
nodes.statement_short: The series converges uniformly, defining an analytic function.

nodes.name: First equation
nodes.statement: By uniqueness of analytic continuation, we get the first equation.
nodes.statement_short: Analytic continuation gives the first equation.

nodes.name: Derivatives
nodes.statement: The rest follows from the polynomial increase of $(s-s_0)^n \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n})$ and Cauchy's integral formula for derivatives.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy's integral formula for the derivatives.

nodes.name: Gamma_0(N) case
nodes.statement: We treat the case for $\Gamma_0(N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Treat $\Gamma_0(N)$.

nodes.name: First column and Bezout coefficients
nodes.statement: Take any $A \in {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$. Let the first column of $A$ be $(a_1,\cdots,a_r)^T \in \ag{Z}^r$. Then we have ${\rm lcd}(a_1,\cdots,a_r)=1$, which implies the existence of $u_i \in \ag{Z}$ such that $\Sigma_{i=1}^r u_i a_i = 1$. In particular, we have ${\rm lcd}(u_1,a_2,\cdots,a_r)=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $A$ and Bezout coefficients $u_i$ for its first column.

nodes.name: Dirichlet's theorem
nodes.statement:
For any $k_j \in \ag{Z}, 2 \leq j \leq r$, the substitution
	$$ u_1' = u_1+\sum_{j=2}^r k_j a_j; u_j' = u_j-k_j, 2 \leq j \leq r $$
	still gives $\Sigma_{i=1}^r u_i' a_i = 1$. By an iterative application of Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progression, we can choose $k_j$'s such that $u_1'$ is a prime number as large as we want. In particular, we can make ${\rm lcd}(u_1',N)=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Modify the $u_i$ so that $u_1'$ is a large prime, coprime to $N$.

nodes.name: Second Bezout relation
nodes.statement: Since ${\rm lcd}(u_1',\cdots,u_r')=1$, at least one of $u_j', 2 \leq j \leq r$, say $u_2'$, is coprime with $u_1'$. Hence ${\rm lcd}(u_1',Nu_2')=1$ and we can find $v_1,v_2 \in \ag{Z}$ such that $u_1'v_2-Nu_2'v_1=1$.

nodes.name: Matrix B in Gamma_0(N)
nodes.statement:
The matrix
	$$ B = \begin{pmatrix} u_1' & u_2' & u_3' \cdots \\ Nv_1 & v_2 & 0 \cdots \\ \vec{0} & \vec{0} & I_{r-2} \end{pmatrix} \in \Gamma_0(N) $$
	and gives, for some $A'=\tilde{A}-\vec{\alpha} \vec{\beta_1}^T \in {\rm SL}_{r-1}(\ag{Z})$, that
	$$ BA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \vec{\beta_1}^T \\ \vec{\alpha} & \tilde{A} \end{pmatrix} \Rightarrow A \in \Gamma_0(N) \begin{pmatrix} 1 &  \\ \vec{\alpha} & A' \end{pmatrix} n_r^+(\vec{\beta_1}). $$
nodes.statement_short: Build $B\in\Gamma_0(N)$ clearing the first column.

nodes.name: Induction on r
nodes.statement:
Repeating the process on $A'$ or making an induction on $r$ we then find successively $\vec{\beta_k} \in \ag{Z}^{r-k}$ such that for some lower unipotent $N_-^1$
	$$ A \in \Gamma_0(N) N_-^1 N_+^1, N_+^1=\prod_{k=0}^{r-2} \begin{pmatrix} I_k & 0 \\ 0 & n_{r-k}^+(\vec{\beta_{k+1}}) \end{pmatrix}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Iterate to get $A\in\Gamma_0(N)N_-^1N_+^1$.

nodes.name: Reduce mod N
nodes.statement: Taking $N_-$ resp. $N_+$ with off-diagonal entries lying in $[-\frac{N}{2}, \frac{N}{2}] \cap \ag{Z}$ such that $N_-^1 \equiv N_- \pmod{N}$ resp. $N_+^1 \equiv N_+ \pmod{N}$, we then find $N_-^1 N_-^{-1}, N_+^1 N_+^{-1} \in \Gamma(N)$ and conclude by its normality.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce entries mod $N$ and use normality of $\Gamma(N)$.

nodes.name: Part (1)
nodes.statement:
(1) On $\ag{R}^{r_1} \times \ag{C}^{r_2}$ we have a usual norm $\Norm_2$ given by
	$$ \Norm[\vec{x}]_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{r_1+r_2} \norm[x_i]^2}, \vec{x}=(x_i)_{1 \leq i \leq r_1+r_2}. $$
	We then easily see, essentially by comparing $f_c$ with the infinity norm, that
	$$ \sup_{\vec{x}} f_c(\vec{x}) \Norm[\vec{x}]_2^c \leq (r_1+r_2)^{\frac{c}{2}}. $$
	If $\alpha_i \in \mathfrak{J}^{-1}$ is an integral basis such that $\mathfrak{J}^{-1}=\Sigma_{i=1}^r \ag{Z} \alpha_i$, then $\sigma(\alpha_i)$ is a basis of the lattice $\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1})$. We can define another norm $\Norm_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}$ by
	$$ \Norm[\vec{x}]_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^r n_i^2}, \vec{x} = \sum_{i=1}^r n_i \sigma(\alpha_i) \in \ag{R}^r. $$
	Or equivalently, if we write $A_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}=(\sigma(\alpha_1), \cdots, \sigma(\alpha_r)) \in {\rm GL}_r(\ag{R})$, we have
	$$ \Norm[\vec{x}]_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}} = \Norm[A_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}^{-1}\vec{x}]_2. $$
	Fix a basis $\vec{e_i}$ of $\sigma(\mathfrak{o})$ and write $A_{\mathfrak{o}}=(\vec{e_1},\cdots,\vec{e_r})$. By elementary divisor theorem, there are $\gamma,\gamma_{\mathfrak{J}} \in {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$ and some $d_i \in \ag{Z}-\{0\}, d_i \mid d_{i+1}, \norm[d_1 \cdots d_r] = \norm[\mathfrak{o}/\mathfrak{J}] = \norm[\mathfrak{J}^{-1} / \mathfrak{o}]$, such that
	$$ A_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}^{-1} = \gamma {\rm diag}(d_1,\cdots,d_r) \gamma_{\mathfrak{J}} A_{\mathfrak{o}}^{-1}. $$
	Changing $\gamma$ is equivalent to changing the choice of basis $\alpha_i$ for $\mathfrak{J}^{-1}$. Applying Lemma \ref{CongGpLemma}, we can find $\gamma$ such that
	$$ {\rm diag}(d_1,\cdots,d_r)^{-1} \gamma {\rm diag}(d_1,\cdots,d_r) \gamma_{\mathfrak{J}} = N_+ N_- $$
	where $N_+$ resp. $N_-$ is upper resp. lower unipotent with entries lying in $[-\frac{d_r}{2d_1}, \frac{d_r}{2d_1}]$. We thus get a bound of the operator norm
	$$ \Norm[A_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}^{-1}]_2 = \Norm[{\rm diag}(d_1,\cdots,d_r) N_+N_- A_{\mathfrak{o}}^{-1}]_2 \leq \norm[d_r] \left( r+\frac{r(r-1)d_r^2}{8d_1^2} \right) \Norm[A_{\mathfrak{o}}^{-1}]_2. $$
	We finally estimate and conclude by
\begin{align*}
	\sum_{\alpha \in \mathfrak{J}^{-1} - \{0\}} f_c(t\sigma(\alpha)) &= \sum_{\alpha \in \mathfrak{J}^{-1} - \{0\}} \Norm[t\sigma(\alpha)]_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}^{-c} \frac{\Norm[t\sigma(\alpha)]_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}^c}{\Norm[t\sigma(\alpha)]_2^c} f_c(t\sigma(\alpha)) \Norm[t\sigma(\alpha)]_2^c \\
	&\leq t^{-c} \norm[d_r]^c \left( r+\frac{r(r-1)d_r^2}{8d_1^2} \right)^c \Norm[A_{\mathfrak{o}}^{-1}]_2^c (r_1+r_2)^{\frac{c}{2}} \sum_{\vec{n} \in \ag{Z}^r-\{0\}} \Norm[\vec{n}]_2^{-c}.
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Compare $f_c$ with lattice norms.

nodes.name: Euclidean norm
nodes.statement:
(1) On $\ag{R}^{r_1} \times \ag{C}^{r_2}$ we have a usual norm $\Norm_2$ given by
	$$ \Norm[\vec{x}]_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{r_1+r_2} \norm[x_i]^2}, \vec{x}=(x_i)_{1 \leq i \leq r_1+r_2}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\|\cdot\|_2$.

nodes.name: f_c vs norm
nodes.statement:
We then easily see, essentially by comparing $f_c$ with the infinity norm, that
	$$ \sup_{\vec{x}} f_c(\vec{x}) \Norm[\vec{x}]_2^c \leq (r_1+r_2)^{\frac{c}{2}}. $$
nodes.statement_short: $f_c(\vec x)\|\vec x\|_2^c$ is bounded.

nodes.name: Lattice norm
nodes.statement:
If $\alpha_i \in \mathfrak{J}^{-1}$ is an integral basis such that $\mathfrak{J}^{-1}=\Sigma_{i=1}^r \ag{Z} \alpha_i$, then $\sigma(\alpha_i)$ is a basis of the lattice $\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1})$. We can define another norm $\Norm_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}$ by
	$$ \Norm[\vec{x}]_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^r n_i^2}, \vec{x} = \sum_{i=1}^r n_i \sigma(\alpha_i) \in \ag{R}^r. $$
	Or equivalently, if we write $A_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}=(\sigma(\alpha_1), \cdots, \sigma(\alpha_r)) \in {\rm GL}_r(\ag{R})$, we have
	$$ \Norm[\vec{x}]_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}} = \Norm[A_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}^{-1}\vec{x}]_2. $$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the norm attached to a basis of $\mathfrak J^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Elementary divisors
nodes.statement:
Fix a basis $\vec{e_i}$ of $\sigma(\mathfrak{o})$ and write $A_{\mathfrak{o}}=(\vec{e_1},\cdots,\vec{e_r})$. By elementary divisor theorem, there are $\gamma,\gamma_{\mathfrak{J}} \in {m SL}_r(\ag{Z})$ and some $d_i \in \ag{Z}-\{0\}, d_i \mid d_{i+1}, 
orm[d_1 \cdots d_r] = 
orm[\mathfrak{o}/\mathfrak{J}] = 
orm[\mathfrak{J}^{-1} / \mathfrak{o}]$, such that
	$$ A_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}^{-1} = \gamma {m diag}(d_1,\cdots,d_r) \gamma_{\mathfrak{J}} A_{\mathfrak{o}}^{-1}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Elementary divisor decomposition of the basis change.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5.35
nodes.statement:
Changing $\gamma$ is equivalent to changing the choice of basis $\alpha_i$ for $\mathfrak{J}^{-1}$. Applying Lemma \ref{CongGpLemma}, we can find $\gamma$ such that
	$$ {\rm diag}(d_1,\cdots,d_r)^{-1} \gamma {\rm diag}(d_1,\cdots,d_r) \gamma_{\mathfrak{J}} = N_+ N_- $$
	where $N_+$ resp. $N_-$ is upper resp. lower unipotent with entries lying in $[-\frac{d_r}{2d_1}, \frac{d_r}{2d_1}]$. We thus get a bound of the operator norm
	$$ \Norm[A_{\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}^{-1}]_2 = \Norm[{\rm diag}(d_1,\cdots,d_r) N_+N_- A_{\mathfrak{o}}^{-1}]_2 \leq \norm[d_r] \left( r+\frac{r(r-1)d_r^2}{8d_1^2} \right) \Norm[A_{\mathfrak{o}}^{-1}]_2. $$
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\gamma$ via Lemma 5.35 to bound the operator norm.

nodes.name: Sum estimate
nodes.statement_short: Compare the sum with $\sum\|\vec n\|^{-c}$.

nodes.name: Part (2)
nodes.statement:
(2) If $\mathcal{L}$ is a lattice in $\ag{R}^r$ with a basis given by the column vectors in a matrix $A_{\mathcal{L}} \in {\rm GL}_r(\ag{R})$, we define its diameter $d(\mathcal{L})$ associated to this basis as the diameter of the fundamental parallelogram spanned by this basis, i.e.,
	$$ d(\mathcal{L}) = \max_{-1 \leq \lambda_i \leq 1, 1\leq i \leq r} \Norm[A_{\mathcal{L}} \vec{\lambda}]_2. $$
	Thus we have obviously $d(\mathcal{L}) \leq \sqrt{r} \Norm[A_{\mathcal{L}}]_2$. The same argument in the last part of (1) gives, for some choice of basis of $\mathfrak{J}^{-1}$, that
	$$ d(\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1})) \leq \sqrt{r} \Norm[A_{\mathfrak{o}}]_2 \norm[d_1]^{-1} \left( r+\frac{r(r-1)d_r^2}{8d_1^2} \right). $$
	It is also easy to see that for $\vec{x},\vec{y}$ in the same translate of a parallelogram $\vec{x_0}+\mathcal{P}$ of $t\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1})$, we have
	$$ \frac{f_c(\vec{x})}{f_c(\vec{y})} \leq 2^{2r_2c} \left( \frac{r_1+r_2+\sqrt{r}d(t\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1}))}{r} \right)^{rc}. $$
	We thus conclude by
\begin{align*}
	{\rm Vol}(\ag{R}^r/t\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1})) \sum_{\alpha \in \mathfrak{J}^{-1}} f_c(t\sigma(\alpha)) &\leq 2^{2r_2c} \left( \frac{r_1+r_2+t\sqrt{r}d(\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1}))}{r} \right)^{rc} \int_{\ag{R}^r} f_c(\vec{x}) d\vec{x} \\
	&\ll_{\mathbf{F},c} \left( 1+t\frac{\norm[\mathfrak{o}/\mathfrak{J}]^2}{\sqrt{r}} \right)^{rc}.
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Compare the lattice sum with an integral.

nodes.name: Diameter of a lattice
nodes.statement:
(2) If $\mathcal{L}$ is a lattice in $\ag{R}^r$ with a basis given by the column vectors in a matrix $A_{\mathcal{L}} \in {\rm GL}_r(\ag{R})$, we define its diameter $d(\mathcal{L})$ associated to this basis as the diameter of the fundamental parallelogram spanned by this basis, i.e.,
	$$ d(\mathcal{L}) = \max_{-1 \leq \lambda_i \leq 1, 1\leq i \leq r} \Norm[A_{\mathcal{L}} \vec{\lambda}]_2. $$
	Thus we have obviously $d(\mathcal{L}) \leq \sqrt{r} \Norm[A_{\mathcal{L}}]_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the diameter of a fundamental parallelogram.

nodes.name: Bound the diameter
nodes.statement:
The same argument in the last part of (1) gives, for some choice of basis of $\mathfrak{J}^{-1}$, that
	$$ d(\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1})) \leq \sqrt{r} \Norm[A_{\mathfrak{o}}]_2 \norm[d_1]^{-1} \left( r+\frac{r(r-1)d_r^2}{8d_1^2} \right). $$
nodes.statement_short: Bound the diameter of $\sigma(\mathfrak J^{-1})$.

nodes.name: Ratio on a parallelogram
nodes.statement:
It is also easy to see that for $\vec{x},\vec{y}$ in the same translate of a parallelogram $\vec{x_0}+\mathcal{P}$ of $t\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1})$, we have
	$$ \frac{f_c(\vec{x})}{f_c(\vec{y})} \leq 2^{2r_2c} \left( \frac{r_1+r_2+\sqrt{r}d(t\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1}))}{r} \right)^{rc}. $$
nodes.statement_short: $f_c$ varies by a bounded factor on each parallelogram.

nodes.name: Sum vs integral
nodes.statement_short: Bound the sum by the integral of $f_c$.

nodes.name: Section of the norm
nodes.statement:
The following exact sequence is split with a splitting section $s: \ag{R}_+ \to \ag{A}^{\times}$
	$$ 1 \to \ag{A}^{(1)} \to \ag{A}^{\times} \xrightarrow{|\cdot|_{\ag{A}}} \ag{R}_+ \to 1 $$
	such that the image of $s$ is contained in $\ag{A}_{\infty}^{\times} = \prod_{v \mid \infty} \mathbf{F}_v^{\times}$. For any $t \in \ag{R}_+$, we write $t^+=s(t)$ with $t_v^+=t^{1/r} \in \ag{R}_+ \subset \mathbf{F}_v$, such that
	$$ |t^+|_{\ag{A}} = \prod_{v \mid \infty} |t_v^+|_v = t. $$
nodes.statement_short: Fix the archimedean section $t\mapsto t^+$.

nodes.name: Classical route
nodes.statement: We may apply the compactness of $\mathbf{F}^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}^{(1)}$, or proceed alternatively in the following more classical way.
nodes.statement_short: Proceed via the class group.

nodes.name: Class group representatives
nodes.statement: Let ${\rm Cl}(\mathbf{F})$ be the class group of $\mathbf{F}$ and choose an integral ideal $\tau$ in each class $[\tau] \in {\rm Cl}(\mathbf{F})$. Let $\delta_{\tau} \in \ag{A}_{{\rm fin}}^{\times}$ be a representative of $\tau$ in the group of ideles. Since ${\rm Cl}(\mathbf{F}) \simeq \mathbf{F}^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}_{{\rm fin}}^{\times} / \widehat{\mathfrak{o}}^{\times}$, there is a unique $\tau$, and some $\beta=\beta_0 u \in \mathbf{F}^{\times}$ with freely chosen $u \in \mathfrak{o}^{\times}$ such that $ y_{{\rm fin}} \in \beta \delta_{\tau} \widehat{\mathfrak{o}}^{\times}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $y_{fin}\in\beta\delta_\tau\hat{\mathfrak o}^\times$.

nodes.name: Normalize y
nodes.statement_short: Compute the archimedean norms of $\beta^{-1}y$.

nodes.name: Dirichlet's unit theorem
nodes.statement: By Dirichlet's unit theorem, we can adjust $u \in \mathfrak{o}^{\times}$ so that each $\norm[u^{-1}\beta_0^{-1}y_v' ]_v$ remains in a compact set in $\ag{R}_+$ depending only on $\mathbf{F}$.
nodes.statement_short: Adjust by units to keep archimedean components bounded.

nodes.name: Reduce to lattice sum
nodes.statement:
We thus find
\begin{align*}
	&\quad \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbf{F}^{\times}} \prod_{v\mid \infty} \min(|\alpha y_v|_v^{-c_1},|\alpha y_v|_v^{-c_2}) \prod_{v<\infty} |\alpha y_v|_v^{-c_1} 1_{v(\alpha y_v) \geq -\mathfrak{c}(\psi_v)-v(\mathfrak{J})} \\
	&= \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbf{F}^{\times}} \prod_{v\mid \infty} \min(|\alpha \beta^{-1} y_v|_v^{-c_1},|\alpha \beta^{-1} y_v|_v^{-c_2}) \prod_{v<\infty} |\alpha \delta_{\tau}|_v^{-c_1} 1_{v(\alpha) \geq -\mathfrak{c}(\psi_v)-v(\mathfrak{J} \tau)} \\
	&= t^{-c_1} \sum_{\alpha \in (\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{F}} \mathfrak{J} \tau)^{-1} - \{0\}} \prod_{v\mid \infty} \min(1,\norm[\alpha t_v^+]_v^{-(c_2-c_1)} \cdot \norm[u^{-1}\beta_0^{-1}y_v']_v^{c_1-c_2}) \\
	&\ll_{\mathbf{F},c_2-c_1} t^{-c_1} \sum_{\alpha \in (\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{F}} \mathfrak{J} \tau)^{-1} - \{0\}} f_{c_2-c_1}(t^{\frac{1}{r}} \sigma(\alpha)).
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the sum as a lattice sum of $f_{c_2-c_1}$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5.36
nodes.statement: We then apply Lemma \ref{GTechEstClassical} to conclude.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by Lemma 5.36.

nodes.name: Constant term product
nodes.statement:
We continue to use the notations in the previous lemma. We can write
	$$ {\rm E}_{\gp{N}}(s,f_1) {\rm E}_{\gp{N}}^{(1)}(0,f_2) = 2(f_1f_2)_{1/2+s}^{(1)} + 2(\mathcal{M}_s f_1f_2)_{1/2-s}^{(1)} + (f_1 \mathcal{M}_0^{(1)}f_2)_{1/2+s} + (\mathcal{M}_s f_1 \mathcal{M}_0^{(1)}f_2)_{1/2-s}. $$

Taking Laurent expansions, we verify that the function in $s$ in the range of the above limit is regular at $s=0$, unlike its appearance. The properties
	$$ {\rm P}_{\gp{K}}(f_1 \mathcal{M}_0^{(k)}f_2) = {\rm P}_{\gp{K}}(f_2 \mathcal{M}_0^{(k)}f_1), \forall k \in \ag{N}; \quad \mathcal{M}_0^{(2)} = \mathcal{M}_0^{(1)} \circ \mathcal{M}_0^{(1)} $$
	$$ \text{coming from} \quad \mathcal{M}_s \circ \mathcal{M}_{-s} = 1 $$
must be used.

nodes.name: Constant terms of E^reg
nodes.statement:
We can write
	$$ {\rm E}_{\gp{N}}^{{\rm reg}}(s,f) = f_s + (\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_s f)_{-s} + \lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(s-\frac{1}{2}) {\rm P}_{\gp{K}}(f) \left( e_{-s} - e_{-1/2} \right); $$
\begin{align*}
	{\rm E}_{\gp{N}}^{{\rm reg},(n)}(\frac{1}{2},f) &= f_{1/2}^{(n)} + \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} (-1)^k (\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{1/2}^{(n-k)} f)_{-1/2}^{(k)} \\
	&+ {\rm P}_{\gp{K}}(f) \cdot \left\{ \frac{(-1)^{n+1} \lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^{-1)}(0)}{n+1} e_{-1/2}^{(n+1)} + \sum_{k=1}^n \binom{n}{k} (-1)^k \lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^{(n-k)}(0) e_{-1/2}^k \right\},
\end{align*}
from which one easily deduce ${\rm E}_{\gp{N}}^{{\rm reg}}(1/2+s,f_1) {\rm E}_{\gp{N}}^{{\rm reg},(n_2)}(1/2,f_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Write constant terms of $E^{reg}$ and its derivatives.

nodes.name: Tentative E^reg(s)
nodes.statement:
We tentatively define
\begin{align*}
	\mathcal{E}^{{\rm reg}}(s) &:= {\rm E}^{(n_2)}(\frac{3}{2}+s, f_1f_2) + \sum_{k=0}^{n_2} \binom{n_2}{k} (-1)^k {\rm E}^{{\rm reg}, (k)}(\frac{1}{2}+s, f_1 \widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{1/2}^{(n_2-k)} f_2) \\
	&\quad + {\rm P}_{\gp{K}}(f_2) \cdot \left\{ \frac{(-1)^{n_2+1} \lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^{(-1)}(0)}{n_2+1} {\rm E}^{{\rm reg},(n_2+1)}(\frac{1}{2}+s, f_1) \right. \\
	&\quad \left. + \sum_{k=1}^{n_2} \binom{n_2}{k} (-1)^k \lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^{(n_2-k)}(0) {\rm E}^{{\rm reg},(k)}(\frac{1}{2}+s, f_1) \right\} \\
	&\quad + {\rm E}^{{\rm reg},(n_2)}(\frac{1}{2}-s, f_2 \widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{1/2+s}f_1) \\
	&\quad + \lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(s) {\rm P}_{\gp{K}}(f_1) \cdot \left\{ {\rm E}^{{\rm reg},(n_2)}(\frac{1}{2}-s, f_2) - {\rm E}^{{\rm reg},(n_2)}(\frac{1}{2}, f_2) \right\}.
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Define $\mathcal E^{reg}(s)$.

	$$ {\rm P}_{\gp{K}}(f_1 \widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{1/2}^{(k)}f_2) = {\rm P}_{\gp{K}}(f_2 \widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{1/2}^{(k)}f_1), \forall k \in \ag{N} $$

orm[y_v]_v^{ rac{1}{2}-
